title: Spain vs. England Player Ratings: La Roja’s Historic Undefeated Streak Finally Broken
subtitle: SI
paragraphs: By Jamie Spencer5:41 PM ESTEngland is leaving Spain with a win. / Eddie Keogh/The FA/Getty ImagesSpain lost a soccer match for the first time in more than two years on Sunday, beaten 3–2 by England in a statement victory for the Three Lions in the UEFA Nations League to top Group A3.

An English victory looked more nailed on than it actually was in the end, when Harry Kane’s penalty late in the first half was followed early in the second by further goals from Arsenal defenders Ezri Konsa and Ben White.

But then the drama began. Elliot Anderson sent off conceding a penalty scored by Mikel Oyarzabal, before substitute Nico Williams reduced England’s lead and set up a tense final 15 minutes in the Spanish capital, where La Roja hadn’t lost in 39 years prior to kick off.

England started like a bullet train and only point-blank reflexes from 2026 Yashin Trophy winner Unai Simón prevented Jude Bellingham from giving the visiting Three Lions a lead inside 90 seconds. Anthony Gordon was also denied immediately after by a vital block.

England’s press kept putting Spain under pressure deep in their own territory and Kane almost benefited with a shot that flashed only inches wide. Not eight minutes were on the clock, but Spain rode out that initial storm and it soon became a more even contest.
Spain’s increasing influence on proceedings didn’t match England’s early fury, unsurprisingly more patient and methodical as the passes soon racked up.

Still, the lead by halftime was no less than England deserved. The challenge from Pau Cubarsí on Kane was clumsy at best and around four minutes had passed between referee Clément Turpin pointing to the penalty spot and a VAR review ruling on Spain’s flimsy appeal for a free kick in the buildup—Anderson’s through ball to Kane saw follow-through contact on Marc Cucurella but in no way could be considered a foul on the Spain left back.
Kane duly fired past Simón from 12 yards.

Harry Kane had missed a penalty when Spain previously won at Wembley. / Alejandro Matias/PS Images/MB Media/Getty ImagesLuis de la Fuente was mad enough after seeing his team largely stifled by an impressive England game plan up to that point that he made a triple substitution at halftime. Added to the enforced earlier injury replacement of right back Marc Pubill, the Spain manager had burned through four of his permitted subs with half the match still to play.

But England was clearly emboldened by the way the first half ended and scored a second eight minutes into the second. It was a goal straight from the Arsenal training pitch, with Declan Rice’s corner finding the head of an unmarked Konsa in the middle of Spain’s box. England was then in dreamland just moments later when White’s overlapping run saw the right back played in by  Bellingham, finishing with conviction through Simón’s legs.

Then, it threatened to collapse. Out of nowhere, Anderson brought down Lamine Yamal and was red carded for the denial of a goalscoring opportunity. James Trafford was rushing out—would he have got to the ball anyway without Anderson’s tug? Maybe. Either way, it didn’t matter because Oyarzabal scored the subsequent penalty.

Spain pulled back a second goal when Jarell Quansah was caught on the ball in England territory. A first-time pass across the box from Yamal later, Williams was wheeling away in celebration. That made for a tremendously nervous final 15 minutes, as Spain pushed for an equalizer and England, down a man, tried to hang on.
Trafford was called into action several times in the second half, but no save proved more important than a world-class stop to deny Aymeric Laporte off of an initial Fermín López shot.

England managed to see it through this time. / Michael Regan/The FA/Getty ImagesWhere was this England performance in the World Cup semifinals?

Thomas Tuchel’s team threw away a place in the 2026 World Cup final that day, leading the contest against Argentina by a single goal but conceding twice in the closing moments to lose the match. The stakes weren’t exactly the same—this was not the World Cup and both teams had already qualified for the Nations League quarterfinals in March. But the England performance made it seem like there has been growth nonetheless.

Initially, here, England didn’t make its brilliant start count. Early chances came and went without being converted and it then seemed only a matter of time before Spain would take control of the ball and pass them into submission.

Kane, fresh from his Ballon d’Or win last month, scored a pressure penalty when he’d missed one that could have changed the outcome in England’s 3–2 defeat to Spain in September. Kane doesn’t often miss from 12 yards, but you’ll recall he also missed under pressure against France in the 2022 World Cup quarterfinals.

For Spain, the consequences aren’t huge. The world champion will theoretically have a slightly tougher quarterfinal draw due to England topping the standings on goal difference, but will ultimately still back itself to beat anyone in its path.

The more disappointing aspect from a Spanish point of view is that the undefeated streak is over at 43 matches—a world record all the same. Spain’s last defeat, excluding penalty shootouts, had been on March 22, 2024. It hadn’t lost a competitive international match in even longer, since March 28, 2023, when Scott McTominay scored twice for Scotland in a Euro 2024 qualifier in Glasgow.
